opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the headline story in open models has been this race at the frontier. Who releases the biggest mixture-of-experts model, who tops the leaderboard, whether open weights are six months or twelve months behind the closed labs. That's important, but I don't think it's where most of the actual value ends up.

What I expect is that the ecosystem gets a lot more stratified. You'll have a handful of organizations, a few Chinese labs, maybe Meta or whoever picks up that mantle, and some well-funded nonprofits, that can afford to train truly frontier-scale open models. Then underneath that there's a much larger layer of people taking those models and distilling them, fine-tuning them, and specializing them. I think the small model space, say one to thirty billion parameters, is where the most interesting open work will happen. Those models run on a laptop or a single GPU, companies can actually own them, and you can do real research on them without a giant cluster.

The other big piece is post-training. With reinforcement learning, especially RL with verifiable rewards, the recipe for turning a base model into something useful has become much more important and much more accessible. A small team with good data and a good RL setup can take an open base model and make something very competitive in math, code, or a specific domain. So I think open source shifts from "who has the biggest pretrained model" to "who has the best recipes, the best data, and the best tooling." That's a big reason we've pushed hard on fully open releases at Ai2, with the data, training code, and intermediate checkpoints, because that's what lets the research community build on it, not just download weights.

And then there's the question of what "open" even means. A lot of what's called open source today is really open weights with restrictive licenses and no data transparency. I think there'll be growing pressure, from academics and from governments thinking about AI sovereignty, for genuinely open models where you can see what went in. Countries and companies that don't want to depend on a single American or Chinese API provider are going to care a lot about that.

So my picture is: the frontier race keeps going and gets a lot of attention, but the real ecosystem is the long tail of smaller, specialized, well-documented models and the open infrastructure around them, like datasets, evaluation tools, and RL frameworks. That's where you get a healthy scientific community instead of just a few companies throwing weights over the wall.

r001.rationale: The response says small models can run on a laptop or single GPU, but does not compare their cost for repeated tasks with continually using Claude or Codex.

r002.rationale: It predicts a shift from asking who has the biggest pretrained model toward better recipes, data, tooling, and smaller specialized models, indicating that the fixation on the largest models will diminish.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing people get wrong is they look at open source through the lens of the frontier, right? Like, who's closest to the closed labs. And that's a real question, but it's actually a pretty small slice of what's going on.

The way I'd frame it is that open models are winning in the middle and the bottom of the distribution way faster than at the top. If you look at what people are actually deploying, the volume is in these 1 to 10 billion parameter models, sometimes smaller. Things that run on a laptop, on a phone, on a single cheap GPU. And that's where openness has a structural advantage, because you can fine-tune it, you can quantize it, you can distill it, you can inspect it. A closed API just can't give you that.

So one direction I'm pretty confident about is specialization. Instead of one giant generalist, you get a bunch of models that are really good at one domain. Code, or a particular language, or biology, or whatever. And the base models get commoditized. Honestly I think that's already happening. The base model is becoming more like infrastructure, like Linux, and the interesting work moves up the stack to post-training, data, and the tooling around it.

The second thing is the ecosystem of components, not just weights. Datasets, evaluation suites, training recipes, RL environments. That's where I spend a lot of my time, and I think it's underrated. Releasing weights without the recipe is kind of like open source software without the build system. You can use it, but you can't really reproduce it or improve it. The groups that release the whole pipeline are the ones actually moving the field.

And then the third piece is geography and institutions. A lot of the most interesting open models right now aren't coming from US big tech. They're coming from Chinese labs, from Europe, from academic and nonprofit groups. That's healthy, but it also means the question of what open means, and who sets the norms, is going to get more contested, not less.

So my short answer is: the frontier will stay mostly closed for a while, and I don't think that's the real story. The story is that everything below the frontier is becoming open by default, and the value shifts to who can take an open base and make it genuinely useful for a specific problem.

r001.rationale: The response says small models can run on a cheap GPU, but does not state that using them for repeated tasks costs less than continually using Claude or Codex.

r002.rationale: It predicts that the frontier will remain mostly closed and says the larger story is open models below the frontier, with value shifting to specialized uses. This communicates a shift away from fixation on the largest models.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll see a much broader ecosystem of smaller, specialized models. The biggest models get most of the attention because they’re easy to compare on benchmarks, but a lot of useful applications don’t need that scale. They need something inexpensive to run, easy to customize, and reliable at a particular task.

Open models let people experiment with that tradeoff. You can take a model, adapt it to your domain, and deploy it on infrastructure you control. So I’d expect more activity around the whole process: better training data, fine-tuning tools, evaluations, and ways to run models efficiently.

The interesting question becomes less ‘Does this open model beat the best closed model at everything?’ and more ‘Can someone build something useful with it that they couldn’t build before?’ There’s a lot of room for that beyond the largest models.

r001.rationale: It says smaller models can be inexpensive to run, but does not compare repeated use with continually using Claude or Codex.

r002.rationale: It predicts growth in smaller, specialized models, but does not clearly predict that the community’s focus on the largest models will diminish.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll see a lot more specialization. Right now, the conversation is dominated by who has the biggest model and who’s closest to the frontier on benchmarks. But a lot of the value in open models is going to come from smaller models that people can adapt to a particular problem, run cheaply, and actually control.

For example, if you’re building a coding tool or working in a specific language, you may not need the best general-purpose model. You need something that does your task reliably, with the latency and cost that make sense for your product. Open models let people experiment with that entire stack, from the training data to fine-tuning to deployment.

So I expect the ecosystem to become more diverse. There will still be a few organizations training very large models, but around them you’ll have people creating specialized versions, improving the tooling, and figuring out what works in practice. The interesting question becomes less ‘Who has the biggest model?’ and more ‘What can people build with it?’

r001.rationale: The response says smaller models can run cheaply, but does not connect that advantage to repeated tasks or compare it with continually using Claude or Codex.

r002.rationale: It predicts the discussion will shift from who has the biggest model toward what people can build, indicating that the community’s fixation on the largest models will diminish.
